text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Visits to the doctor are too expensive for many Stockholm residents who earn less than 100,000 crowns a year. A quarter of householders surveyed said there had been times in the past year when they had been sick but could not afford to go to the doctor.
- Unemployment amongst immigrants in Sweden is four times higher than among people born in Sweden even though an eighth of companies are run by immigrants, a new study found.
- Prime Minister Goran Persson promised Finance Minister Erik Asbrink would give an answer about the government's views on Sweden's EMU membership in May.

- Handelsbanken indicated that this year will be tougher for banking than last year but that the profit level will be high. Handelsbanken posted a 14 percent lift in profit before credit losses for the first quarter of 1997 of 1.86 billion crowns, in line with expectations. Reduced credit losses boosted profit but the bank can probably not lower them any further.
- The post office wants to put a stop to manual sorting, closing down four of the six terminals that sort manually.

- People are fleeing from the Social Democratic party. Since the 1994 election the party, that has a minority government in Sweden, has lost 57,000 members, almost a fifth of its membership. The exodus is connected to the party's economic policies, a study finds.

- A key issue for Volvo's development this year will be its truck division. Volvo, due to release its first quarter results on Wednesday, had a tough 1996 but 1997 has started better, said Volvo Truck chief Karl-Erling Trogen. The company is making money in South America and working hard to turn negative trends in North America.
- Hufvudstaden has a new chief from parent company Custos. Tomas Billing, a 34-year old economist, is the new managing director, moving from being a director at Custos.

- Swedish drugs group Astra reported first quarter earnings of 3.46 billion crowns, a rise of one percent, and its shares fell. Sales for the period only rose nine percent, partly owing to stockpiling by patients and wholesalers prior to year-end 1996.

- Swedbank said in a new report that the Baltic states achieved robust growth in 1996 and reported steadily declining inflation. In the Baltic region, Poland performed the best in 1996 with GDP up six percent. Poland is Sweden's second fastest growing import market after China.

- The National Audit Bureau (RRV) gave low passing grades for financial management to 61 public sector bodies and failed 19. RVV's latest survey of state-owned agencies and public corporations is the first since 1995.

- Swedish investment company Active will divide its operations into two business areas, one anchored by SBL Vaccin, the vaccine company that Active is seeking to acquire from the Swedish state that will be the drive for the company's biotechnology industry.

- The government's alcohol retailing monopoly Systembolaget has been accused of breaking the law against alcohol advertising in Sweden - a law the current president of Systembolaget helped form. The furor revolves around window displays with posters advertising various export-strength beer brands with the slogan "It's just as good with beer". In 1996 the government appointed legal adviser Nils-Olof Berggren to reevaluate the laws.
